summary.text: Coenzymes are complex organic molecules that act as helpers for enzymes, and they are one of the two types of cofactor.
They are mainly derived from vitamins and other organic essential nutrients.
Some stay tightly bound as prosthetic groups, while cosubstrates attach only briefly and can be released and rebind later.

facts.value: An apoenzyme is an enzyme without its cofactor

facts.label: Complete enzyme
facts.value: Enzyme plus cofactor is a holoenzyme

items.prompt: A scientist removes the helper molecule from an enzyme, and the enzyme goes inactive. What is the inactive form called?
items.explain: An inactive enzyme without its cofactor is an apoenzyme; the complete enzyme with cofactor is a holoenzyme.

items.prompt: A helper molecule is so tightly attached that it is hard to remove without ruining the enzyme. What can it be called?
items.explain: A cofactor that is difficult to remove without denaturing the enzyme can be called a prosthetic group, unlike cosubstrates that are only transiently bound.

items.prompt: Where do most of the organic helper molecules that enzymes need come from?

options.label: Extra copies of the enzyme itself

items.explain: Coenzymes are mainly derived from vitamins and other organic essential nutrients.

items.prompt: ATP, coenzyme A, FAD and NAD⁺ all contain AMP. What has been suggested about that shared part?

options.label: It may supply the metal ion the enzyme needs
It may act as a handle the enzyme can grasp
It may stop the coenzyme binding at all
It may turn the substrate into a vitamin

items.explain: The AMP part may be a kind of handle by which the enzyme can grasp the coenzyme and switch it between catalytic centers.

items.prompt: Nutrition lists of essential trace elements reflect their role as enzyme cofactors in humans. Which of these is commonly on that list?
items.explain: The human list commonly includes zinc, while chromium has no known enzyme use, iodine goes into thyroid hormones, and calcium activates enzymes by allosteric regulation rather than as a cofactor.

items.prompt: Heme proteins have a cofactor with both an inorganic and an organic part. What are they?
items.explain: Heme proteins consist of a porphyrin ring coordinated to iron, a cofactor with both an inorganic and an organic component.

paragraphs.heading: Helpers for enzymes
paragraphs.text: An enzyme may need a partner before it can act as a catalyst. That partner is a cofactor: a chemical compound or metal ion, not made of protein, that the enzyme requires in order to work. You can think of cofactors as helper molecules that assist chemical changes inside living things. Cofactors come in two kinds, inorganic ions and complex organic molecules, and those organic helpers are called coenzymes.

paragraphs.heading: Where coenzymes come from
paragraphs.text: Most coenzymes are made from vitamins and other essential organic nutrients needed in small amounts. Organic cofactors are often vitamins themselves or are built from them. Many of them share one building block, a nucleotide called adenosine monophosphate, or AMP. It appears inside ATP, coenzyme A, FAD and NAD⁺. This shared piece may point to a shared origin, as parts of ribozymes in an ancient RNA world.

paragraphs.heading: Tight or loose
paragraphs.text: Coenzymes split into two groups by how they hold on. A prosthetic group stays tightly attached to its protein, sometimes by a covalent bond that makes the link permanent. A cosubstrate attaches only for a while: it can be let go and then bind again later. Both kinds do the same job, which is to help enzymes and proteins carry out their reactions. Still, there is no sharp line between loosely and tightly bound helpers.

paragraphs.heading: Switching the enzyme on
paragraphs.text: Without its cofactor, an enzyme sits idle, and in that state it is called an apoenzyme. Once the cofactor is in place, the complete working enzyme is called a holoenzyme. Organic cofactors are small molecules, usually under 1000 Da in mass, and they take a direct part in the reaction. One idea is that the AMP part works like a handle the enzyme grips to move the coenzyme between different working sites.

paragraphs.heading: Many helpers at once
paragraphs.text: Some enzymes or groups of enzymes need several cofactors together. Pyruvate dehydrogenase, a cluster of enzymes that links glycolysis to the citric acid cycle, is a good example. It needs five organic cofactors and one metal ion. They include thiamine pyrophosphate, held loosely; lipoamide and FAD, bound covalently; the cosubstrates NAD⁺ and coenzyme A; and the metal Mg²⁺.

paragraphs.heading: A word with blurry edges
paragraphs.text: Different sources define a coenzyme in slightly different ways, and the terms are often used loosely. Some call tightly bound organic molecules prosthetic groups rather than coenzymes, while others call every non-protein organic helper a coenzyme. The International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry, or IUPAC, describes a coenzyme as a small, loosely attached organic compound that carries chemical groups or electrons and can come off. A 1980 letter in a biochemistry journal went further and suggested the word coenzyme be dropped altogether, since no single definition seemed to fit.
